name: Bitter candytuft (Iberis amara), in a six-herb preparation
short: Nine-herb version with greater celandine: acute severe hepatitis (1 case). Six-herb product without celandine: severe or related adverse events as with placebo. No data on candytuft alone.
text: This entry covers bitter candytuft (Iberis amara) only as part of a six-herb liquid preparation taken by mouth, which contains extracts of bitter candytuft, chamomile (matricaria) flower, peppermint leaves, caraway, licorice root and lemon balm, and no greater celandine. No human safety data were found for bitter candytuft on its own; a 2002 review reports only laboratory and rodent tests, in which the fresh plant extract at therapeutic doses showed no cytotoxic or acute toxic action. The six-herb preparation: a 2024 meta-analysis of individual patient data identified four randomized controlled trials (613 patients), analysed safety by odds ratios for all adverse events, and found that treatment-related or severe adverse events did not differ from placebo; the abstract does not say how many of the trials the safety analysis used. In an 8-week double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial in 272 people with functional dyspepsia, safety parameters did not differ between groups (the abstract does not list the events). In a 4-week trial in 186 people that compared it with cisapride and with the nine-herb version, tolerability and safety parameters were secondary endpoints and showed no statistically significant differences. The abstract of a 120-patient placebo-controlled trial gives no safety results. The 272-patient and 186-patient trial abstracts identify the preparation only by a product code, not repeated here, which the meta-analysis abstract gives for the six-herb combination. Related product (not the six-herb preparation): a nine-herb version contains extracts of bitter candytuft, chamomile flower, peppermint leaves, caraway fruit, licorice root, lemon balm leaves, angelica root, celandine herb (the abstract does not name the species) and milk thistle fruit. A case report describes acute severe hepatitis with jaundice in a 32-year-old woman taking a preparation of 9 plant extracts including greater celandine, resolving 5 weeks after stopping, and the authors note occasional earlier cases of liver injury with it; the case report identifies the preparation by a brand name, not repeated here, that ties it to this nine-herb version. Greater celandine has its own entry. The preparation contains licorice root; the cited abstracts do not report blood pressure or potassium. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy or children. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
